newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Vibrant Hong Kong seen maintaining financial edge.
newsitem.headline: Vibrant Hong Kong seen maintaining financial edge.

text.p: One of the world's most vibrant and open economies has made Hong Kong a key hub for East Asia and under Chinese rule it looks set keep a competitive edge and fend off any challenge from fast-growing Shanghai.

Polls regularly show that both Hong Kong Chinese and the millions of foreign business people who drop in here for a few days or for a lifetime are confident about the future after Britain hands the colony back to China on June 30.
But nobody expects life to remain exactly the same.

"The question is not whether there will be concessions, but will they be substantial enough to knock a very robust economy off the rails," said David Dodwell, a director at Jardine Fleming and co-author of the book "The Hong Kong Advantage."

Dodwell said Hong Kong enjoys so many more freedoms, both financial and political, than many of its Asian neighbors that its freedoms would have to be "substantially eroded" before it would lose out to Singapore or Taiwan, for example.

While China has angered democracy campaigners in Hong Kong and raised the hackles of Western leaders by diluting political rights, Beijing repeately has that it will not meddle with the financial future of the hugely successful capitalist enclave.

Under the Basic Law hammered out between Britain and China, Beijing has promised to allow Hong Kong to maintain for 50 years the freewheeling capitalist way of life that has made the territory of 6.3 million people an economic powerhouse.
Hong Kong is the world's seventh largest merchandise trading economy and boasts foreign reserves of US$63.6 billion, among the highest in the world.
Growth is forecast at a healthy 5.5 percent in 1997 and per capita gross domestic product is an impressive US$26,000.
Hong Kong's wealth is no secret. It has more Rolls-Royces and cellular phones per head than anywhere else on Earth and the territory is the biggest importer of cognac.

Dodwell said it is very difficult to change the minds of people who are sure that Chinese officials will violate the Basic Law, in the same way that it is almost impossible to shake the confidence of those that consider the vow unbreakable.
"Some people believe and some people don't," he said.
Clearly, China has good reasons to make sure Hong Kong maintains its good name in international markets.
Hong Kong accounts for some 60 percent of all realised direct external investment in China, according to the Hong Kong government's most recent data.

China's desire to reunite Taiwan with the mainland also gives it a strong incentive to make sure everything goes right in Hong Kong, said Andrew Freris, managing director, Asia Research, at Bank of America.

Hong Kong's Chief-Executive designate Tung Chee-hwa earlier this year sent out strong signals that his new government may not deviate sharply from its predecessor by retaining many of the colonial government's top bureaucrats.
The decision was viewed as a vote for stability.
Analysts said Tung will need to send out more signals if he wants to allay another widely-held fear -- that corruption and influence peddling may take hold after the handover.
"The number one concern among our clients is whether Hong Kong can hold the line on corruption," said Stephen Vickers, senior managing director at risk management firm Kroll Associates (Asia) Ltd.

Mark Sundberg, chief regional economist at Salomon Brothers, said that as other Chinese cities improve their infrastructure, Hong Kong will become less attractive as a trading center because of its relatively high costs.
But few believe that Shanghai or other Chinese cities can even hope to vie successfully with Hong Kong for years to come.

Edgar Cheng, chairman of Hong Kong's stock exchange, said that Shanghai cannot compete with Hong Kong at least until China's currency becomes fully covertible, something that is not expected to happen for years.
Jardine's Dodwell said he was "astonished that people take seriously the issue of Shanghai being a commercial threat to Hong Kong as a financial centre."

Dodwell said Shanghai possesses none of the four strengths -- the rule of law, low taxes, lack of government interference and the free movement of people, capital and information -- that have always made Hong Kong so alluring to business.
